Project 01 · Digital banking

Moving money should feel fast. Trust should never feel rushed.

Redesigning AIB’s Pay & Transfer journey across payee setup, IBAN validation, instant payments, authentication and limit recovery, turning a fragmented banking task into one coherent payment system.

RoleSenior Product Designer
ScopeDiscovery, product strategy, interaction, UI, prototyping, design system
PlatformiOS & Android
DomainPayments, risk, authentication

Section

Context

A high-frequency banking journey where speed, confidence and risk meet.

Pay & Transfer sits at the center of everyday banking. Customers use it to move money between accounts, pay someone new and complete time-sensitive transfers. The challenge was not simply reducing steps. It was making every step explain what was happening before money moved.

14
Core states
Designed across the end-to-end prototype, including recovery and authentication.
4
Critical moments
Payee setup, validation, transfer feedback and daily-limit recovery.

Section

What existed / What I redesigned

The product already moved money. The redesign made the journey behave like one system.

Existing experience
Functional, but fragmented

Static IBAN guidance, limited inline feedback, contact payments outside the primary path and a daily limit that behaved like a dead end.

Redesigned experience
Guided, contextual and recoverable

Real-time validation, instant payment visibility, explicit feedback, strong authentication and recovery embedded at the moment it is needed.

Section

Evidence before solutions

The benchmark was useful only when it explained a customer expectation.

Revolut, N26, Monzo and Pix were not references to copy. They helped establish what customers already understood as normal: immediate validation, contact-based payments, visible status and recoverable limits.

01
Validation before commitment

Customers should know whether an IBAN is valid before submitting the form.

02
Identity before account detail

When possible, choosing a person should feel closer to messaging than filling a bank form.

03
Guardrails need exits

A security limit can protect customers without forcing a support call.

Section

Design principle

Make the safe path also the fast path.

In payments, speed and safety are not opposite goals. The strongest experience removes uncertainty early, makes system status visible and introduces friction only when risk actually increases.

I reframed Pay & Transfer as a payment system rather than a sequence of screens.

Section

Daily limit strategy

A security limit should stop risk, not stop the customer.

The daily limit was the clearest example of the product principle.

Scenario
Customer needs to send €14,000 · Daily limit €10,000
OPTION A

Block

Stop the transfer and direct the customer to support.

Low exposure · Low autonomy
OPTION B

Permanent increase

Raise the ceiling and keep it higher for future transfers.

High autonomy · Higher lasting exposure
DECISION · C

Temporary elevation

Strong authentication, time-bounded increase and automatic reset.

Autonomy with bounded exposure
CUSTOMER
Complete now

No support call for a legitimate high-value transfer.

RISK
Bound exposure

The higher ceiling exists only for a defined window.

SECURITY
Verify intent

Strong authentication protects the change in risk.

SYSTEM
Reset automatically

The safer default returns without another customer action.

€14k requested→Limit detected→Temporary increase→Face ID→Continue transfer→Auto reset

Section

Risk × friction

Not every financial action deserves the same amount of friction.

I used risk as a trigger for friction instead of spreading security steps across the whole journey.

ActionRiskProduct response
Choose saved payeeLOWNo additional friction
Add a new IBANMEDIUMReal-time account validation
Send standard transferMEDIUMReview and standard confirmation
Increase daily limitHIGHStrong authentication + time-bound change
High-value transferHIGHExplicit review + elevated assurance
Security should not add friction everywhere. It should appear where risk changes.

Section

Designing trust

Trust is not a confirmation screen. It is accumulated across the journey.

For a payment to feel trustworthy, the product needs to answer a different question before, during and after money moves.

BEFORE

Am I sending the right money to the right person?

Recipient identity · IBAN · receiving bank · amount · payment rail

DURING

Is the bank actually processing my instruction?

Authentication · locked CTA · processing state · duplicate prevention

AFTER

Did the money move, and can I prove it?

Outcome · timestamp · reference · receipt · recovery when uncertain

TRUST BUILDS THROUGHIdentity→Validation→Review→Authentication→Status→Receipt

Section

Decision 01

Decision 01

Validate the IBAN while the customer is still able to fix it.

Problem

Static guidance delayed error discovery until submit.

Decision

Validate structure in real time, identify the receiving bank when possible, and make the error actionable.

Trade-off

More system feedback on the form, but less uncertainty at the point of commitment.

Section

Decision 02

Decision 02

Make paying a person a primary action, not a feature customers have to discover.

Problem

Contact payment lived behind setup. The capability existed, but discoverability and entry cost weakened its value.

Decision

Contact becomes a first-class payee type. The interaction starts with customer intent, who are you paying, and the system resolves the rail behind that choice.

Trade-off

A contact-first entry point means someone paying a first-time payee without a phone-linked account still needs the manual or IBAN path. It cannot fully disappear.

Section

Decision 03

Decision 03

Every step that touches money should answer: did that work?

Feedback is not decoration in a payment flow. It is part of the customer’s mental model of whether money is safe, pending or complete.

Problem

Fields filled in silently before, with nothing confirming a step had gone well.

Decision

A purpose-built confirmation for each moment: a live SEPA Instant toggle while entering the amount, and a real receipt once the payment lands.

Trade-off

More design surface to build and maintain than a single generic loading state.

Section

Interaction detail

Recovery flow

Turn the limit from a dead end into a controlled recovery path.

Problem

A higher limit increases exposure and requires stronger confidence in identity, but a hard wall forces a support call for a legitimate high-value transfer.

Decision

A self-service temporary increase: pick an amount, re-confirm with Face ID, done in under a minute, reverting automatically after 24 hours.

Trade-off

A temporary increase that reverts automatically could surprise someone who expected it to stay. The copy has to carry that weight.

Section

Trade-offs

Senior design happens where two good goals conflict.

Speed × Security
Flexibility × Fraud exposure
Automation × Customer control
Minimal UI × Explicit feedback

The goal was not to eliminate friction. It was to make friction proportional to risk and useful to the customer.

Section

Cross-functional decisions

The strongest decisions were negotiated at the boundary between customer experience, risk and system behaviour.

DESIGN × ENGINEERING

IBAN validation

Question
When can the product confidently identify an account?

Constraint
Validation may be asynchronous or temporarily unavailable.

Outcome
Checking, valid, invalid and unable-to-verify became explicit product states.

DESIGN × PRODUCT × RISK

Daily limit

Question
How do we unblock legitimate high-value transfers?

Constraint
A permanent increase expands exposure beyond the immediate need.

Outcome
Temporary elevation, strong authentication and automatic reset.

DESIGN × SECURITY × ENGINEERING

Authentication

Question
Where should stronger authentication appear?

Constraint
Repeated security prompts make routine payments unnecessarily heavy.

Outcome
Authentication appears when risk changes, while transaction context is preserved.

Collaboration was not a handoff step. It changed the shape of the product.

Section

Final experience

One customer task. Five stages. Thirteen screens. One coherent payment system.

The final experience is organized around the customer’s mental model, while validation, payment rails, risk, authentication and transaction states are coordinated underneath.

01ChooseSaved · Contact · New
02IdentifyIBAN · Bank · Eligibility
03TransferAmount · Rail · Review
04SecureRisk · Limit · Face ID
05ResolveProcessing · Receipt · Recovery
Design intent

Keep the surface simple without hiding the system. Each screen exposes only the decision the customer can make now, while preserving enough context to understand what will happen to their money next.

Section

Components & states

A component is useful when it expresses product state, not only visual style.

The system maps UI variants to what the payment product knows at that moment. That keeps behaviour consistent across the journey and gives Engineering a predictable contract.

IBAN FIELD

Account validation

default → focus → checking → valid → invalid → unavailable

UI mirrors whether the account is unknown, being checked, identified or unresolved.

PAYEE

Recipient identity

saved → contact → new → selected → unavailable

Different entry paths resolve into one recipient model.

PAYMENT RAIL

Transfer eligibility

SEPA → instant available → selected → unavailable

Availability is a product condition, not a decorative toggle.

AMOUNT

Risk boundary

default → filled → approaching limit → over limit

The amount component becomes a risk surface when thresholds change.

AUTHENTICATION

Intent verification

idle → required → authenticating → verified → failed

Security state stays connected to the transaction being approved.

PRIMARY CTA

Submission control

default → disabled → loading → locked → complete

CTA behaviour prevents accidental resubmission while state is unresolved.

FEEDBACK

System communication

info → success → warning → recoverable error

Feedback communicates consequence and next action, not just severity.

TRANSACTION

Money movement

draft → processing → completed → failed → unknown

Transaction status is treated separately from interface/network status.

SYSTEM PRINCIPLE

The component reflects the state of the product. Variants exist because behaviour changes, not because a Figma file needs more options.

Section

Edge-case system

Recovery was designed as part of the payment architecture, not after the happy path.

ScenarioPreventCommunicateRecover
Invalid IBANValidate before commitmentExplain what is wrongEdit inline, preserve value
Instant unavailableCheck rail eligibilityExplain timing changeContinue with SEPA
Limit exceededCheck before submissionShow available limitTemporary elevation
Authentication failedKeep transaction contextExplain verification failureRetry authentication safely
Transfer processingLock duplicate submissionShow explicit statusWait for known state
Connection lostPreserve transaction intentAcknowledge uncertaintyCheck transaction status before retry

Prevent when possible. Explain when necessary. Recover without making the customer rebuild the transaction.

Section

Transaction certainty

In payments, uncertainty can be more damaging than failure.

A failed transfer has a clear meaning. A lost connection after confirmation creates a harder question: did the money move? The interface should never encourage a second submission until the transaction state is known.

01Confirm

Customer commits.

02Lock

CTA cannot submit twice.

03Process

Transaction is pending.

04Resolve

Check authoritative status.

05Recover

Retry only when safe.

STATE LOGIC
review
↓
authenticating
↓
processing ──→ completed → receipt
│
├──→ failed → safe retry
└──→ unknown → status check → resolve

Section

Accessibility

When money is moving, accessibility is part of transaction safety.

The goal was not a generic accessibility checklist. Critical information had to remain understandable when colour, motion, vision or fine motor interaction could not be assumed.

€5,000.00Amount

Hierarchy, label and formatting communicate the value. Size or colour never carries meaning alone.

!Invalid IBAN

Error uses icon, text and actionable guidance, not red alone.

✓Transfer completed

Success is explicit in copy and announced as a state change, rather than depending on green feedback.

•••Processing

Loading has a textual status, prevents duplicate action and does not rely on animation to explain what is happening.

Face IDAuthentication failure

Failure preserves context and provides a clear recovery route instead of restarting the payment.

44px+Interaction

Primary actions use comfortable touch targets, visible focus and predictable order across the journey.

Section

Prototype & handoff

High fidelity was not the end of the design. Behaviour was part of the specification.

01
Prototype

Thirteen core states connected end to end: happy path, limits, validation, authentication and recovery.

02
Component behaviour

Default, focus, valid, invalid, loading and disabled. Shared interaction logic reduces one-off implementation.

03
Engineering handoff

State logic, error handling, transition rules and accessibility notes. Design intent remains visible beyond static screens.

04
QA

Visual and interaction review against designed states. Edge cases checked with the same rigor as the happy path.

Section

Engineering handoff

The handoff described behaviour, not just pixels.

For a payment flow, the critical implementation detail is often what happens between screens: when validation fires, what is preserved after failure, when an action locks, and how the product resolves an uncertain transaction.

Behaviour specification
01Validate IBAN asynchronously and expose Checking before a result is known.
02Preserve recipient, amount and payment context after recoverable errors.
03Lock the primary action while a transfer is processing to prevent duplicate intent.
04Do not offer Retry until the previous transaction state is known.
05Return from authentication to the same transaction context.
06Expire the temporary limit automatically after the defined window.
Transaction state
review
↓
authenticating
↓
processing
├─ completed → receipt
├─ failed → recovery
└─ unknown → status check

Design QA checks the implementation against state logic, not only visual parity.

Section

Measurement framework

Success means more customers moving money confidently without assisted recovery.

I defined measurement around the behaviour the redesign was intended to change. This separates product success criteria from metrics that belong to broader AIB work.

NORTH STAR
Successful self-service transfers
01CompletionTransfer completion rate
02SpeedMedian time to complete
03QualityIBAN errors · duplicate attempts
04RecoverySelf-service limit recovery
05ConfidencePost-transfer confidence / CSAT
What I would watch

A faster flow is not automatically a better flow. I would read completion together with validation errors, duplicate attempts, support contacts and recovery rate to make sure speed is not being bought with uncertainty or risk.

Reflection

The fastest payment flow is the one where the customer never has to wonder if it worked.

This project reinforced a principle I carry into complex financial products: simplicity is not removing information. It is deciding what the customer needs to know, when they need to know it, and designing the system so recovery feels intentional rather than exceptional.
